sections.title: Sex on Screen
sections.description:
For much of the twentieth century, moviegoing brought strangers into bodily proximity in a dark, anonymous space, an arrangement that early anti-cinema campaigners regarded as sexually dangerous. What forms of desire did this ritual of shared proximity in the dark produce? Was moviegoing itself, as its earliest critics feared, a kind of perversion—and what changes when public, collective looking becomes solitary and private? How has film theory drawn on psychoanalysis to grasp the desire at work in looking? And how has Italian cinema, from the silent diva to Guadagnino, staged sex and desire as its subject? As streaming platforms progressively displace the shared experience of the darkened movie theater, this seminar asks what happens to the forms of looking and desire that cinema has historically produced.
This course has two main aims: 1) to offer a genealogy of Italian film history from the silent era to the present, focusing on those films that contribute to our knowledge of the mechanics of looking as connected to gender and sexuality; 2) to introduce students to crucial texts and topics in film theory, feminist theory, and queer theory such as scopophilia, voyeurism, and fetishism (Freud, Lacan, Metz); the apparatus and the dark hall as dream-space (Barthes, Baudry); the male gaze and its feminist and queer revisions (Mulvey, Doane, Silverman, Bersani, Edelman).
Throughout, Italian films will be placed alongside key global art films, so that the questions at the heart of the course are pursued across cinematic traditions rather than confined to a single national frame. Films may include Love Everlasting (Mario Caserini, 1913), Blow-Up (Michelangelo Antonioni, 1966), Death in Venice (Luchino Visconti, 1971), Amarcord (Federico Fellini, 1974), Seven Beauties (Lina Wertmüller, 1975), and Suspiria (Dario Argento, 1977), alongside international works such as Rear Window (Alfred Hitchcock, 1954), Peeping Tom (Michael Powell, 1960), Cure (Kiyoshi Kurosawa, 1997), Beau Travail (Claire Denis, 1999), and Goodbye, Dragon Inn (Tsai Ming-liang, 2003), among others. Films will be shown at in-person group screenings scheduled outside class hours.
No knowledge of queer theory, film theory, or Italian is required.
